question: How teams that run PostgreSQL in production monitor XID age and prevent wraparound: the queries they run and their real output, alert thresholds they use, per-table autovacuum tuning, and what holds the oldest-XID horizon back (long or idle-in-transaction sessions, prepared transactions, replication slots, standby feedback). Must find: worked examples with real inputs and outputs, and at least one first-hand incident report.

sources.rank_basis: tier B: class (company engineering blog; Sentry's own post-mortem of its July 2015 outage)
tier B: class (vendor engineering blog, Crunchy Data)
tier B: class (vendor product docs; its facts are about PostgreSQL, not about pganalyze itself)

facts.summary: AWS gives a query on pg_database that lists the 20 databases with the highest age(datfrozenxid), as the count of unfrozen transactions per database.
facts.quote: You can use the following query to show the number of unfrozen transactions in a database. … SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY age(datfrozenxid) desc limit 20;

loc.heading: Determining if the tables in your database need vacuuming

facts.summary: The page shows illustrative output of that query (it says the results "might be" these), with mydb at an age of 1,771,757,888 and template0 at 1,721,757,888.
facts.quote: For example, the results of running the preceding query might be the following. datname | age mydb | 1771757888 template0 | 1721757888 template1 | 1721757888

loc.heading: Determining if the tables in your database need vacuuming

facts.summary: The page states that wraparound occurs and the database becomes read-only when a database's age reaches 2 billion transaction IDs.
facts.quote: When the age of a database reaches 2 billion transaction IDs, transaction ID (XID) wraparound occurs and the database becomes read-only.

loc.heading: Determining if the tables in your database need vacuuming

facts.summary: The query can feed a metric run a few times a day; by default autovacuum keeps transaction age at no more than 200,000,000 (autovacuum_freeze_max_age).
facts.quote: You can use this query to produce a metric and run a few times a day. By default, autovacuum is set to keep the age of transactions to no more than 200,000,000 (autovacuum_freeze_max_age).

loc.heading: Determining if the tables in your database need vacuuming

facts.summary: The sample monitoring strategy starts by setting autovacuum_freeze_max_age to 200 million transactions.
facts.quote: A sample monitoring strategy might look like this: Set the autovacuum_freeze_max_age value to 200 million transactions.

loc.heading: Determining if the tables in your database need vacuuming

facts.summary: A table at 500 million unfrozen transactions triggers a low-severity alarm in that strategy, as a sign that autovacuum may not be keeping up.
facts.quote: If a table reaches 500 million unfrozen transactions, that triggers a low-severity alarm. This isn't an unreasonable value, but it can indicate that autovacuum isn't keeping up.

loc.heading: Determining if the tables in your database need vacuuming

facts.summary: A table aged 1 billion should be treated as an alarm to act on; the page adds that ages should in general stay close to autovacuum_freeze_max_age for performance.
facts.quote: If a table ages to 1 billion, this should be treated as an alarm to take action on. In general, you want to keep ages closer to autovacuum_freeze_max_age for performance reasons.

loc.heading: Determining if the tables in your database need vacuuming

facts.summary: A table at 1.5 billion unvacuumed transactions triggers a high-severity alarm that AWS recommends resolving immediately, since time to run autovacuum may be running out.
facts.quote: If a table reaches 1.5 billion unvacuumed transactions, that triggers a high-severity alarm. Depending on how quickly your database uses transaction IDs, this alarm can indicate that the system is running out of time to run autovacuum. In this case, we recommend that you resolve this immediately.

loc.heading: Determining if the tables in your database need vacuuming

facts.summary: A table that keeps breaching the thresholds calls for further autovacuum tuning; a manual VACUUM runs without cost-based delays, so it is more aggressive but more intrusive than default autovacuum.
facts.quote: If a table is constantly breaching these thresholds, modify your autovacuum parameters further. By default, using VACUUM manually (which has cost-based delays disabled) is more aggressive than using the default autovacuum, but it is also more intrusive to the system as a whole.

loc.heading: Determining if the tables in your database need vacuuming

facts.summary: For busier tables AWS recommends a regular manual vacuum freeze in a maintenance window, on top of autovacuum.
facts.quote: For busier tables, perform a manual vacuum freeze regularly during a maintenance window, in addition to relying on autovacuum.

loc.heading: Determining if the tables in your database need vacuuming

facts.summary: Sentry's post of July 23, 2015 reports that hosted Sentry was down for most of the US working day on Monday, July 20, because of Postgres XID wraparound.
facts.quote: David Cramer - July 23, 2015 … On Monday, July 20th, Sentry was down for most of the US working day.

facts.summary: The post states that Postgres stops accepting commands when fewer than one million transactions are left before the maximum XID value.
facts.quote: To protect you from this, Postgres will stop accepting commands when there are fewer than one million transactions left before the maximum XID value is reached.

facts.summary: Sentry describes its workload as very write-heavy with very large tables, and says its goal had been to vacuum as aggressively as possible.
facts.quote: Sentry is a very write-heavy application. On top of that, we have some very large relational tables (both in number of rows, as well as physical size on disk). … Our goal is to vacuum as aggressively as possible so that this situation should never arise.

facts.summary: Once wraparound protection is active, the post says the only option without data loss is to stop writes and vacuum, with the common advice to restart in single-user mode.
facts.quote: Once Postgres kicks in its XID wraparound protection, unless you’re willing to accept data loss, your only option is to stop accepting writes and vacuum the relations. One piece of general advice is to stop the database and restart in single-user mode, thus running vacuum in a more isolated and safe environment.

facts.summary: During the outage the team chose to let the running autovacuums finish rather than interrupt them to add memory or switch to single-user mode.
facts.quote: At this point we had to make a bet: it was better to let autovacuum finish with our current configuration than to risk interrupting it.

facts.summary: One of the autovacuums failed or did not work, and the cause was unclear because autovacuum logging was not verbose.
facts.quote: Eventually, the autovacuums finish. Unfortunately one of them either failed or simply didn’t work correctly. It’s unclear as to what happened, as the logs contain nothing to suggest failure and we didn’t have verbosity for autovacuums.

facts.summary: While protection was active Sentry ran read-only, with replicas serving reads but no writes accepted.
facts.quote: Up until this point we were operating in a read-only state. We had replicas online that we could point the application at to maintain that view of the world, but it wouldn’t allow us to accept writes.

facts.summary: Internal statistics showed all relations vacuumed except one very large event-mapping table; Sentry truncated it and was fully restored five minutes later.
facts.quote: By querying Postgres’ internal statistics we identified that the autovacuums actually had finished on all of the relations except one. … With our best estimations, we made the call to truncate the table. Five minutes later, the system was fully restored.

facts.summary: Two days later a test machine on older hardware was still running a single-user-mode vacuum, about 24 hours in.
facts.quote: we’re still watching one of our test machines run a vacuum in single-user mode going on 24 hours.

facts.summary: Sentry names its earlier settings as causes: autovacuum_freeze_max_age too high, the default 3 autovacuum workers, and too much vacuum delay.
facts.quote: We previously ran with too high a value for autovacuum_freeze_max_age and the default of 3 autovacuum workers. Additionally, we had been running with far too much delay in vacuuming which meant lower load on the system, but more idle time in maintenance.

facts.summary: Sentry's configuration after the outage: autovacuum_freeze_max_age 500000000, 6 workers, naptime 15s, cost delay 0, maintenance_work_mem 10GB, vacuum_freeze_min_age 10000000.
facts.quote: Our updated configuration: autovacuum_freeze_max_age = 500000000 autovacuum_max_workers = 6 autovacuum_naptime = '15s' autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0 maintenance_work_mem = '10GB' vacuum_freeze_min_age = 10000000

facts.summary: A later update says maintenance_work_mem had a hard internal limit of 1GB for the relevant vacuum paths, so the extra memory given to it was not used.
facts.quote: maintenance_work_mem has a hard internal limit of 1GB for the relevant paths, and thus our 100GB of memory dedicated to it wasn’t even being used.

facts.summary: Crunchy Data's PGmonitor query reports the oldest age(datfrozenxid) across connectable databases as a percentage of 2,000,000,000 and of autovacuum_freeze_max_age.
facts.quote: The following query is the one that we use at Crunchy Data in our PGmonitor tool to provide very simple data points to trend/alert on. … , max(ROUND(100*(oldest_current_xid/max_old_xid::float))) AS percent_towards_wraparound , max(ROUND(100*(oldest_current_xid/autovacuum_freeze_max_age::float))) AS percent_towards_emergency_autovac

facts.summary: percent_towards_wraparound is the critical alert; its 2 billion bound sits a little below the real exhaustion point, and reaching 100% must be acted on at once.
facts.quote: The percent_towards_wraparound metric is the one that is really critical that an alert be set up for. … This query has a little bit of a buffer in it since the upper boundary it checks (2 billion exactly) is less than the actual max integer value that causes the exhaustion. But it's close enough that this alert hitting 100% should be acted upon immediately.

facts.summary: The post states that reaching exhaustion forces the database to shut down, with downtime of unknown length.
facts.quote: If exhaustion is ever reached, the database will be forced to shut down and could cause an indeterminate amount of downtime in order to be fixed.

facts.summary: percent_towards_emergency_autovac is a second recommended alert, watching for a table reaching autovacuum_freeze_max_age (default 200 million), where a higher-priority autovacuum starts on it.
facts.quote: The percent_towards_emergency_autovac metric is the additional value we recommend monitoring for, especially for systems that have never had this monitored for before … This is a user-tunable value that has a default value of 200 million and when any table's highest TXID value reaches it, a higher priority autovacuum kicks in on that table.

facts.summary: That emergency vacuum runs even with autovacuum disabled and restarts after being cancelled; the author says cancelling it for lock contention is safe, but it keeps restarting.
facts.quote: It is higher priority in the sense that it will run even if autovacuum is disabled and if that vacuum is manually cancelled, it will almost immediately restart again. … If you do run into contention/locking issues and they can be narrowed down to the emergency vacuum being the cause, it's perfectly safe to cancel it to allow your other transactions to finish.

facts.summary: For high transaction rates the author raises autovacuum_freeze_max_age, often to 1 billion, only with wraparound monitored and disk space for the larger pg_xact and pg_commit_ts.
facts.quote: For databases with a high transaction rate, it could be beneficial to increase autovacuum_freeze_max_age to avoid that emergency vacuum period coming around quite so often. The main concern with increasing this is that it can increase the storage requirements in the pg_xact and pg_commit_ts folders in the data directory. … I've often set this value to 1 billion without much issue, but only when I'm sure wraparound is being monitored for and the disk space is available.

facts.summary: The cluster-wide fix is vacuumdb with --all (XID is global), --freeze, and --jobs for parallel vacuums, with a warning that a high --jobs adds IO and WAL.
facts.quote: vacuumdb --all --freeze --jobs=2 --echo --analyze … The --all option ensures all databases are vacuumed since the TXID is a global value. The --freeze option ensures a more aggressive vacuum is run to ensure as many tuples as possible are frozen in that table

facts.summary: Worked example: a per-database age query with output showing postgres at 170,604,895 and mydb at 169,088,197 against an autovacuum_freeze_max_age of 200000000.
facts.quote: SELECT datname , age(datfrozenxid) , current_setting('autovacuum_freeze_max_age') FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC; … postgres | 170604895 | 200000000 mydb | 169088197 | 200000000

facts.summary: Worked example: a per-table age(relfrozenxid) query over tables, TOAST and materialized views with output, the oldest being pg_proc at 170,606,208.
facts.quote: postgres=# SELECT c.oid::regclass , age(c.relfrozenxid) , pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(c.oid)) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n on c.relnamespace = n.oid WHERE relkind IN ('r', 't', 'm') AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_toast') ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 100; … pg_proc | 170606208 | 936 kB

facts.summary: The author generates VACUUM FREEZE statements for the 100 oldest relations from psql, runs them in batches of 100, and aims for at least 50% of autovacuum_freeze_max_age, often 30-40%.
facts.quote: select 'vacuum freeze analyze verbose ' || oid::regclass || ';' from pg_class where relkind in ('r', 't', 'm') order by age(relfrozenxid) desc limit 100; … I usually do it in batches of 100 just to give IO and WAL generation some time to calm down. I'll usually try and get the max XID for any table at least down to 50% of autovacuum_freeze_max_age, usually even down to 30-40% if it's not going to be too much trouble.

facts.summary: Since PostgreSQL 9.6 vacuum can skip all-frozen pages, so once tuned the emergency-autovac alert may be lowered or removed, keeping only the wraparound alert.
facts.quote: PostgreSQL 9.6 introduced a feature that allows vacuum to be able to skip over a page if all tuples inside of it are marked as frozen. … So once you have things tuned well, you could consider this alert a low priority warning or maybe even remove it and just worry about monitoring for wraparound itself.

facts.summary: The author says exhaustion must always be monitored, because reaching it is a guaranteed outage.
facts.quote: it should ALWAYS be monitored for no matter what since reaching it is a guaranteed outage that you may not be ready for.

facts.summary: pganalyze's check runs every 30 minutes and by default raises a warning when the server's xmin horizon was assigned more than 24 hours ago, even if no VACUUM is blocked yet.
facts.quote: Every 30 minutes … Detects when the xmin horizon on the server was assigned more than 24 hours ago and creates an issue with severity "warning". The issue will be created even if no VACUUM is currently blocked by this, as this will potentially block any future VACUUMs.

facts.summary: The xmin horizon marks how far vacuum may clean dead rows; while it lags and does not advance, VACUUMs cannot clean dead rows.
facts.quote: The xmin horizon tells you up to which point the vacuum process can clean up dead rows. When this value is behind and not advancing, VACUUMs will be blocked and will not be able to clean up dead rows.

facts.summary: Some holders such as physical slots affect every database on a server, but a long transaction in one database does not stop cleanup of tables in another database.
facts.quote: Note that while some types of xmin horizon delays affect all databases on a server, such as the xmin for each physical replication slots, in other cases not all databases of a server will be impacted … For example, if the xmin horizon is held back by a long running transaction on database1, Postgres can still clean up dead rows of tables in database2, as the transaction of database1 will never be able to see database2.

facts.summary: Long-running transactions block cleanup; a pg_stat_activity query sorted by the age of backend_xmin or backend_xid finds the holder and its pid.
facts.quote: Long-running transactions may still need to access rows that could otherwise be considered dead, so they can block cleanup. … SELECT pid, datname, usename, state, backend_xmin, backend_xid FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_xmin IS NOT NULL OR backend_xid IS NOT NULL ORDER BY greatest(age(backend_xmin), age(backend_xid)) DESC;

facts.summary: Use pg_cancel_backend for a session running an active query and pg_terminate_backend for one idle in transaction; either rolls back the transaction's writes.
facts.quote: You can cancel it by running either pg_cancel_backend if the transaction is running an active query: … or pg_terminate_backend if the connection state is "idle in transaction". … Note this will roll back the transaction, and discard all data written to the database earlier within that transaction.

facts.summary: With hot_standby_feedback on, a lagging or down replica's physical slot can hold the xmin horizon; an unused slot can be dropped with pg_drop_replication_slot.
facts.quote: With physical streaming replication with hot_standby_feedback is on, when replication is lagging or a replica server is stale (e.g. down), the oldest transaction that the replication slot needs the database to retain can be "stuck", holding back the xmin horizon. … If the replication slot is no longer used, you can remove it by running the following command: SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('<slot_name>');

loc.heading: Lagging or stale physical replication slots

facts.summary: A logical slot whose subscriber stalls on a schema mismatch after a migration holds back the primary's system-catalog xmin until replication resumes.
facts.quote: When the subscriber was unable to replicate data due to a schema mismatch, replication will error and get stale. This causes the xmin of the system catalogs of the primary (publisher) to be held back until replication resumes.

loc.heading: Lagging or stale logical replication slots

facts.summary: With hot_standby_feedback on, standby queries hold back the horizon like primary queries; pg_stat_replication on the primary shows each standby's backend_xmin.
facts.quote: When hot_standby_feedback is on with physical streaming replication, queries on standbys will hold back the xmin horizon just as if they were running on the primary. … SELECT application_name, client_addr, backend_xmin FROM pg_stat_replication ORDER BY age(backend_xmin) DESC;

facts.summary: A prepared two-phase transaction blocks cleanup until committed or rolled back; pg_prepared_xacts sorted by age(transaction) finds it.
facts.quote: A transaction prepared for a two-phase commit will prevent cleanup until it is either committed or rolled back. … SELECT gid, prepared, owner, database, transaction AS xmin FROM pg_prepared_xacts ORDER BY age(transaction) DESC;

facts.summary: A found prepared transaction is ended with COMMIT PREPARED or ROLLBACK PREPARED using its gid.
facts.quote: Once identified, you can either commit or cancel the transaction by running either of commands: COMMIT PREPARED <gid_from_above>; ROLLBACK PREPARED <gid_from_above>;

conflicts.topic: at what XID age writes stop
conflicts.note: AWS docs say read-only at 2 billion; Sentry says commands stop with fewer than one million XIDs left; Crunchy says its 2 billion bound is a little below the real exhaustion point

conflicts.topic: what the database does when XIDs run out
conflicts.note: AWS docs and Sentry's account say read-only; Crunchy says the database is forced to shut down

conflicts.topic: what value of autovacuum_freeze_max_age to run with
conflicts.note: AWS sample strategy sets 200 million; Sentry calls its earlier value too high and moved to 500 million; Crunchy often sets 1 billion, on conditions

conflicts.topic: whether to interrupt a running anti-wraparound autovacuum
conflicts.note: Crunchy says cancelling it for lock contention is safe (it restarts); Sentry, already past the protection limit, chose not to interrupt it; the situations differ
